name: Notre-Dame de Paris
modelNote: Placed on the OpenStreetMap footprint and the published dimensions (127 m long, 48 m wide, vaults at 33 m, roofs at 43 m, towers 69 m, spire 96 m); bays, roses and portals are measured on photos. The portals, the gallery of kings, the west rose and the statues in niches are free photographs from Wikimedia Commons laid on the model with their depth; other carving is simplified, and the first spire's form is interpreted. Inside, the great organ and the choir screens are free photographs too: they show through the section view.

evidence.identity: Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Paris, 6 parvis Notre-Dame – place Jean-Paul-II, 75004 Paris, France (OpenStreetMap way 201611261; Mérimée PA00086250)

sources.read: Dimensions (127 × 48 m, nave 60 m long, central vessel 13 m wide, vaults at 33 m, roofs at 43 m, transept 48 × 14 m, ten nave bays and five choir bays, towers 69 m, spire 96 m, façade 43.5 × 45 m, roses 9.70 m and 13.10 m) and the campaigns: choir 1163–1182 (altar consecrated 19 May 1182), nave 1182–1225, façade from 1208 with the rose level 1220–1225, towers 1240 and 1250, chapels from 1235, transept by Jehan de Chelles and Pierre de Montreuil, chevet buttresses by Jean Ravy 1318–1344, end in 1345; 21 of the 28 kings' heads found in 1977; the fire of 15 April 2019; reopening on 7 December 2024. Inside: a three-level elevation (great arcades on large columns, tribunes 8 m high under their vaults, high windows), double aisles continued as a double ambulatory, sexpartite vaults in the nave; the high altar consecrated on 19 May 1182 by the legate Henri de Château-Marçay and Maurice de Sully, the choir finished in 1177.

Mérimée notice: first stone laid by Maurice de Sully in 1163; choir, nave and aisles 1163–1225; high galleries, spire and towers 1225–1250; transept, roses and chapels later in the Middle Ages; under the Revolution the spire is pulled down and the kings' statues removed, Temple of Reason in 1793; restoration decided in 1844 and given to Viollet-le-Duc and Lassus, who rebuild the spire, invent the chimeras, remake the kings and build a new sacristy; works end on 3 January 1865.

Éduscol (Ministry of Education, April 2019): the choir finished with its frame in 1177 while the old cathedral was pulled down; stone cutters, setters and mortar makers, wood in every structure, lead for cramps and glass; the towers completed in 1245; Jean Ravy's 14th-century flying buttresses; Lassus and Viollet-le-Duc restore the 28 kings, design a new spire of oak covered with lead and replace Soufflot's sacristy; the spire falls on the evening of 15 April 2019, its copper statues removed beforehand.

Rebuilding authority: a thousand oaks for the spire and transept frames, nearly 1,300 m3 of stone; the golden cock set on 16 December 2023, some 96 m above the ground, completing the structural work; the scaffolding of the spire removed in September 2025, revealing the sixteen restored copper statues.

The first spire, built 1220–1230, rose 78 m above the floor and was taken down 1786–1792; Viollet-le-Duc's spire is 96 m high, 18 m more, with about 250 t of lead; sixteen statues (twelve apostles and four evangelist symbols) in four groups, one per roof, facing the cardinal directions, removed four days before the fire; the spire fell at about 7:45 pm on 15 April 2019; the cock was set on the new spire on 16 December 2023.

Vannucci, Structural study of the Notre-Dame ancient charpente (2020): the frame was 115.6 m long, 13 m wide and 9.75 m high over nave and choir; choir frame after 1220 (about 1225–1230), nave frame about 1230–1240, transept, spire and the frames next to it rebuilt by Lassus and Viollet-le-Duc after 1843 on the system of trusses, purlins and rafters; 'chevrons formant fermes': principal trusses (tie beam, king post, collars, struts) with four secondary trusses between them, 4.1 m and 82 cm apart in the choir, 3.5 m and 75 cm in the nave; longitudinal ties and braces join the king posts; roof pitch about 55°; some timbers reused from the first roof of about 1160–1170, whose form is not known.

Rebâtir Notre-Dame: the oak frames and lead roofs of nave, choir and transept burnt on 15 April 2019 and are reconstituted identical to the originals; the nave and choir frames dated from the early 13th century, the spire and transept frames from 1859–1864 by Viollet-le-Duc; logs squared and shaped with adze or axe as in the 13th century; the medieval 'trussed rafter' system alternates complex main trusses with simpler rafters, each truss different; the trusses are covered with sand-cast lead sheets and a lead ridge crest.

Grand orgue de Notre-Dame de Paris: under the west rose; built in its present case by François Thierry in 1733, rebuilt by François-Henri Clicquot in 1783 and by Aristide Cavaillé-Coll in 1868 (86 stops); 115 stops and 7,952 pipes since 2014; not seriously damaged by the 2019 fire but made unusable by soot and dust, it was taken down except its case, bellows and some 10 m pipes, cleaned, reinstalled under the west rose and played at the reopening on 7 December 2024.

Palissy PM75000695, clôture de chœur: painted and gilded stone, 13th century to mid-14th; begun by Jean Ravy and finished by his nephew Jean le Bouteiller; height 220 cm on the south side, 145 cm on the north; north panels from the Visitation to the Mount of Olives, south panels the appearances of Christ after the Resurrection; scraped, repainted and partly completed by Viollet-le-Duc; listed 20 February 1905.

features.text: Harmonic west front: three portals, a gallery of 28 kings, the 9.70 m rose between two tall windows, an open high gallery and two square towers 69 m high.
Two transept fronts, each with a rose 13.10 m across, a glazed gallery, a portal and a gable between slender turrets.
Long single-span flying buttresses around the chevet, built by Jean Ravy in the early 14th century.
Chapels filling the spaces between the buttresses along the nave and around the choir, under small gables.
A steep lead roof on an oak frame, its ridge 43 m above the ground, with a half cone over the apse.
A spire of oak covered with lead, 96 m high, with sixteen copper statues in four groups on the roofs.
Twin lancets under an oculus in the clerestory, above buttress piers crowned with pinnacles.
Two tall louvred openings on each face of the towers, corner buttresses and a balustrade at the top; a stair turret on the north tower.
Viollet-le-Duc's sacristy south of the choir, in the cathedral's style.
The 'forest': the oak roof frame of chevrons formant fermes, a principal truss every 3.5–4.1 m and four rafter trusses between, burnt in 2019 and rebuilt identically.
The great organ under the west rose, on its tribune: case of 1733 by François Thierry, rebuilt by Clicquot (1783) and Cavaillé-Coll (1868), 7,952 pipes.
The choir screens of the 14th century, painted and gilded: the life of Christ on the north side, his appearances after the Resurrection on the south side.
Inside, a three-level elevation: great arcades on large round columns, tribunes over the inner aisles, high windows under sexpartite vaults; double aisles round the nave and choir.

evidence.geometry: Footprint, orientation (axis at azimuth 115.6°) and the positions of the buttresses, transept fronts and apse are measured on OpenStreetMap way 201611261; heights come from the published dimensions; bay counts, roses, portals and the levels of the west front are read from the reference photos.
uncertainties: The first spire (1220–1230, 78 m) is drawn like Viollet-le-Duc's, smaller: its exact form is not documented in the sources used.
The 12th-century flying buttresses, replaced in the 13th and 14th centuries, and the original transept fronts are not modelled in detail; the transept arms show plain ends until the 1250s fronts.

The west front's carving is shown by photographs of 2014 and 2025, laid on the model: the portals appear as they are today in every phase, so their earlier states and the restorations of the 19th century are not shown (only the gallery of kings is taken down under the Revolution and set back afterwards). Other sculpture (the transept portals, the chimeras, the crockets) is simplified.
The sacristy is drawn as three plain blocks on its OpenStreetMap footprint; its height is estimated. Soufflot's earlier sacristy is not shown.
The 2019 collapse of part of the vaults and their rebuilding are not shown.

Seen from the north-east, the model and the photo still differ by about 5% of the photo's height after fitting the viewpoint; the cause (the photo's recorded position or the towers' plan) is not settled.

Inside, only the great organ (on a tribune drawn plainly), the choir screens (their masonry, height above the floor and place along the choir read on photographs) and the high altar of 1182 (form and place not known) are shown; the choir stalls, Robert de Cotte's altar and the Vœu de Louis XIII are not.

The interior elevation is drawn from the published vault height and the tribunes' 8 m: the arcade's springing (7.2 m), the tribune openings and the aisle and chapel vaults (6.5–11 m) are read on photographs, not surveyed; the choir's vaults are drawn sexpartite like the nave's, and the crossing and transept as simple quadripartite bays.

gaps: All four captures show the 2019–2025 state, with the spire hidden in its scaffold, while the photos (2011–2015) show the cathedral restored by Lassus and Viollet-le-Duc: the references must be captured at the end of that phase.

West front (parvis, 2015): the levels match (portals, gallery of kings, rose between two twin windows, open high gallery, towers with two tall louvred openings per face); the photo's portals are deeper, with statues in the jambs, a trumeau and carved tympana, where the first capture showed flat recesses.

South-west (square Viviani, 2011): the tower, the nave's flying buttresses and pinnacles, the chapel gables, the south rose and the spire line up as in the photo; the capture is framed wider than the photo.
North-east (right bank, 2011) and east (2014): the north rose and its gable, the chevet's radiating flying buttresses, the half-cone roof of the apse and the towers behind read as in the photos.
Roofs and the spire first rendered pink and green: the plain materials reused the textured stone shader.
fixed: References captured at the end of the restoration phase ("phase": "restauration").
South-west reference framed with a 38° lens instead of 46°.
Portals: five archivolts through the wall, three jamb statues a side, a trumeau with its statue, doors and a tympanum in registers.
Each material now compiles its own shader program, so lead and glass are no longer tinted by a stray texture; lead darkened to the photos' blue-grey.

gaps: West front: portals, gallery of kings, rose level, high gallery and towers now read level by level as in the photo; the photo's sculpture (jamb statues, tympana, the Virgin and angels before the rose, chimeras) is far richer than the model's simple figures.

South-west (Viviani): tower, flying buttresses, pinnacles, chapel gables, south rose, transept turrets and spire match the photo's composition; the photo's flyers are more slender and the chapel gables sharper.
North-east and east: the north front, the chevet with its radiating flyers and the apse roof read as in the photos; the real chevet flyers leap about 15 m in one span, the model's about 10 m.
The sacristy, hidden by trees and buildings in every photo, cannot be checked against them.
fixed: Each reference viewpoint fitted with calibrate.mjs on points recognised in its photo (tower corners, rose centres, the spire's tip, gable apexes, portal apex): the overlays showed the earlier viewpoints framed too tight and aimed too high.

gaps: West front: with the viewpoint fitted on six points (camera moved 12 m from the recorded position), the model stays within 2.4% of the photo's height; its towers are slightly wider at the top than the real ones, whose balustrades sit inside the corner buttresses.
South-west (Viviani): fitted on five points, within 1.1%; tower, flyers, south rose and spire overlay the photo.

North-east: fitted on five points, the gap stays at 5%: the spire and the north tower land left of the photo's while the gable and the south tower fit, so either the photo's recorded position is far off or the towers' plan near the crossing differs.
East: fitted on six points with the camera moved, within 3.3%; the chevet, its flyers and the apse roof overlay the photo, the towers behind are slightly offset.
fixed: The towers' bases were open behind above the aisle roofs (pass 3, north-east view: the inside of the north tower showed through): they are closed by their east walls, with the arches through which the aisles run on, and by the towers' sides along the terrace.
The bay between the towers had no vault and no cover: the nave's vault now runs on to the west front under the lead terrace, its sides opening through tall arches into the towers' bases.

Seen in section, the choir and nave stood on 22 m columns under a plain barrel that hid the high windows: they now stand on an arcade of round piers with the tribunes' openings above, under sexpartite vaults (rib vaults in the transept and apse) whose wall arches rise over the windows, with rib vaults over the aisles and chapels.
Arches springing at their sill had jambs of no length; lit as NaN, they blackened section views through the bloom. Such pieces are no longer laid.
remaining: Sculpture is reduced to simple figures; tracery is schematic (twin lancets and an oculus per bay, spoked roses).
The chevet's flying buttresses are shorter than the real 15 m spans.
The north-east view keeps a 5% gap after fitting: to be resolved with a better located photo or a measured plan of the towers.
The first spire is interpreted, and the sacristy's height is estimated.

South-west (Viviani): fitted on five points, within 1.1%; tower, flyers, south rose and spire overlay the photo.

East: fitted on six points with the camera moved, within 3.3%; the chevet, its flyers and the apse roof overlay the photo, the towers behind are slightly offset.

phases.title: The choir
phases.text: Bishop Maurice de Sully lays the first stone in 1163. The choir and its double ambulatory are finished with their roof in 1177, and the high altar is consecrated on 19 May 1182.

moments.title: The first stone
moments.text: Maurice de Sully lays the first stone in 1163, in the presence of Pope Alexander III.

moments.title: Cutters, setters, mortar makers
moments.text: Stone cutters, setters and mortar makers share the walls; wood frames every structure on site, and lead seals the iron cramps.

moments.title: The high altar consecrated
moments.text: On 19 May 1182 the papal legate Henri de Château-Marçay and Maurice de Sully consecrate the high altar; the choir was finished in 1177 and mass was said there from 1180.

phases.title: The nave
phases.text: The four eastern bays of the nave rise with their aisles and galleries from 1182, then the western bays. The old cathedral is pulled down as the new one goes up.

moments.title: One cathedral replaces another
moments.text: The earlier cathedral, dedicated to Saint Stephen, is pulled down bit by bit as the new one is built.

moments.title: Vaults 33 m high
moments.text: The nave is 60 m long; its central vessel is 13 m wide under vaults 33 m high.

phases.title: The west front
phases.text: From 1208 the three portals rise, then the gallery of kings and, around 1220–1225, the level of the rose, 9.70 m across.

moments.title: Twenty-eight kings
moments.text: A gallery of 28 statues of kings runs right across the front above the portals.

moments.title: The west rose
moments.text: The rose of the west front measures 9.70 m across.

phases.title: Towers and chapels
phases.text: The high gallery and the two 69 m towers are finished by 1250. Chapels fill the spaces between the nave's buttresses, new flying buttresses carry the vaults and a first spire rises over the crossing.

moments.title: North 1240, south 1250
moments.text: The north tower is finished in 1240 and the south tower in 1250.

moments.title: A first spire, 78 m
moments.text: Built from 1220 to 1230, the first spire reaches 78 m above the floor and also serves as a bell tower.

phases.title: Roses and flying buttresses
phases.text: Jehan de Chelles, then Pierre de Montreuil, lengthen the transept and give it two roses 13.10 m across. Chapels ring the choir, and Jean Ravy builds the chevet's flying buttresses; the works end in 1345.

moments.title: The north rose
moments.text: Jehan de Chelles lengthens the transept around 1250 and builds the north front and its rose.

moments.title: Jean Ravy's flying buttresses
moments.text: Early in the 14th century Jean Ravy builds the flying buttresses that still draw the cathedral's outline.

moments.title: The choir screen
moments.text: Jean Ravy begins the stone screen round the canons' choir, carved and painted with the life of Christ; his nephew Jean le Bouteiller finishes it in 1351.

phases.title: The great organ
phases.text: François Thierry builds the great organ in 1733, in the case that still stands under the west rose, on its tribune at the end of the nave. François-Henri Clicquot rebuilds it in 1783 and Aristide Cavaillé-Coll in 1868; today it has 7,952 pipes.

moments.title: Under the west rose
moments.text: Seen from the nave, the case stands before the rose. The 2019 fire spared it: cleaned pipe by pipe, the organ was played again at the reopening on 7 December 2024.

phases.title: Spire down, kings removed
phases.text: The decaying 13th-century spire is taken down from 1786 to 1792. Under the Revolution the statues of the gallery of kings are removed and the cathedral becomes a Temple of Reason in 1793.

moments.title: Heads found in 1977
moments.text: Of the 28 original heads of the kings, 21 were found in 1977; they are kept at the Musée de Cluny.

phases.title: Lassus and Viollet-le-Duc
phases.text: Restoration is decided in 1844: the kings are carved again, chimeras invented and a new sacristy built. Viollet-le-Duc's oak and lead spire, 96 m high, is inaugurated on 15 August 1859; the works end on 3 January 1865.

moments.title: A sacristy in the cathedral's style
moments.text: Viollet-le-Duc pulls down Soufflot's sacristy and builds a new one imitating the cathedral's architecture.

moments.title: 18 m taller
moments.text: The new spire rises to 96 m, 18 m higher than the first; its lead covering weighs some 250 tonnes.

moments.title: Sixteen copper statues
moments.text: The twelve apostles and the four symbols of the evangelists stand in four groups on the roofs, each facing a cardinal direction.

phases.title: The fire
phases.text: Fire breaks out in the roof at about 6:18 pm. The spire falls at 7:45 pm, breaking part of the vaults; the oak frame and the lead roofs are lost. The sixteen statues had been taken down four days earlier.

moments.title: The spire falls
moments.text: The upper part of the spire collapses around 7:45 pm; its fall destroys part of the nave vaults and the crossing.

phases.title: Rebuilt as it was
phases.text: Frames and spire are rebuilt to the same design with a thousand oaks; the gilded cock crowns the 96 m spire on 16 December 2023. The cathedral reopens on 7 December 2024.

moments.title: The golden cock
moments.text: On 16 December 2023 the golden cock is set on the spire, some 96 m above the ground, completing the structural work.

moments.title: 7 December 2024
moments.text: The cathedral reopens with an official ceremony on 7 December 2024, and to the public the next day.

moments.title: The statues return
moments.text: When the spire's scaffolding comes down in September 2025, the sixteen restored copper statues are back in place.

elements.name: Charpente du chœur (XIIe s.)
elements.note: The first frames, of the 1160s–1210s, are not known: drawn as Viollet-le-Duc read the early Gothic roofs, without tie beams, the rafters held by collars and braces (Vannucci 2020, fig. 4a). Replaced from 1225.

elements.name: Charpente de l'abside (XIIe s.)
elements.note: The first frames, of the 1160s–1210s, are not known: drawn as Viollet-le-Duc read the early Gothic roofs, without tie beams, the rafters held by collars and braces (Vannucci 2020, fig. 4a). Replaced from 1225.

elements.name: Charpente de la nef (vers 1200)
elements.note: The first frames, of the 1160s–1210s, are not known: drawn as Viollet-le-Duc read the early Gothic roofs, without tie beams, the rafters held by collars and braces (Vannucci 2020, fig. 4a). Replaced from 1225.

elements.name: Charpente du chœur (1225–1230)
elements.note: The choir frame of about 1225–1230: 'chevrons formant fermes', a principal truss with tie beam and king post every 4.1 m and four rafter trusses (fermettes) between them, 82 cm apart (Vannucci 2020, survey of Fromont and Trentesaux). Burnt in 2019 and rebuilt identically in green oak hewn with axes.

elements.name: Charpente de l'abside (1225–1230)
elements.note: The choir frame of about 1225–1230: 'chevrons formant fermes', a principal truss with tie beam and king post every 4.1 m and four rafter trusses (fermettes) between them, 82 cm apart (Vannucci 2020, survey of Fromont and Trentesaux). Burnt in 2019 and rebuilt identically in green oak hewn with axes.

elements.name: Charpente de la nef (1230–1240)
elements.note: The nave frame of about 1230–1240: the same system with principal trusses every 3.5 m and four fermettes 75 cm apart (Vannucci 2020). Burnt in 2019 and rebuilt identically in green oak hewn with axes.

elements.name: Charpente du transept (XIIIe s.)
elements.note: The 13th-century transept frame, replaced in the 19th century, is not described in the sources used: drawn like the nave's.

elements.name: Charpente du transept (Viollet-le-Duc)
elements.note: The transept frame and the first frames by the spire, rebuilt by Lassus and Viollet-le-Duc in 1859–1864 on the 19th-century system of trusses, purlins and rafters (Vannucci 2020; Rebâtir Notre-Dame); the spacing of its trusses is drawn at 4 m, not measured. Burnt in 2019, rebuilt identically.

elements.name: Galerie des rois
elements.note: The 28 kings remade under Lassus and Viollet-le-Duc, photographed in 2014; the medieval kings pulled down under the Revolution stood in the same niches.

elements.name: Portail de la Vierge
elements.note: The Virgin's portal: her death and coronation in the tympanum above the lintel of prophets and kings; its doorway is not centred under its arch, as the photo shows.

elements.name: Portail du Jugement dernier
elements.note: The Last Judgement: Christ in judgement above the weighing of souls and the resurrection of the dead on the two lintels, apostles on the jambs.

elements.name: Portail Sainte-Anne
elements.note: St Anne's portal: the Virgin in majesty under a canopy in the tympanum, above two lintels, saints on the jambs.

elements.name: Rose occidentale
elements.note: The west rose, 9.70 m across, with the Virgin and Child between two angels standing on the balustrade before it; photographed in 2014 and set in the rose's opening.

elements.name: Statue en niche
elements.note: One of the four statues standing in niches on the front of the buttresses at the level of the portals, from the 2025 photograph of the front.

elements.name: Rose nord
elements.note: The north transept rose, 13.1 m across, photographed from below in 2017 and straightened: its lowest part, behind the balustrade, is not seen in the photo.

elements.name: Rose sud
elements.note: The south transept rose, 13.1 m across, from a 2010 photograph of the south side; the balustrade before its foot is part of the photo.
The first spire (1220–1230) rose 78 m above the floor; its form is not documented in the sources used, so it is drawn like its successor, smaller.

elements.name: Tribune et buffet d'orgue
elements.note: The tribune at the west end of the nave and the mass of the organ case behind its photograph: the tribune's two columns, the case's depth and its towers' plan are drawn plainly; the case's width and height are read on the photograph, scaled on the west rose (9.70 m).

elements.name: Grand orgue
elements.note: The great organ's case of 1733 with its pipes, before the west rose, photographed from the nave in December 2024 after its restoration; laid on the case at its width and height.

elements.name: Clôture du chœur
elements.note: The masonry of the north and south choir screens, against the choir's piers, behind the photographs of their carving: the base's height (2.5 m to the ledge under the scenes) and the screens' place along the choir are read on photographs, not measured.

elements.name: Clôture nord
elements.note: The west end of the north screen, begun under Jean Ravy: the meal at Bethany, the Entry into Jerusalem, the Last Supper, the Washing of the Feet and the Mount of Olives (its last scene), under their canopy, as Viollet-le-Duc repainted them; 1.45 m from the ledge to the canopy (Palissy) gives the scale.

elements.name: Clôture sud
elements.note: The south screen, finished by Jean le Bouteiller in 1351: Christ appearing to Mary Magdalene, to the holy women, to Peter and to the pilgrims of Emmaus, under its openwork crest; 2.20 m from the ledge to the crest (Palissy) gives the scale. The Commons file is titled north, but these scenes are the south screen's.

elements.name: Maître-autel (1182)
elements.note: The high altar consecrated on 19 May 1182, at the head of the choir: its form and place are not known and are drawn as a plain stone altar on two steps; it was replaced in 1699 by Robert de Cotte's, and is drawn until the 18th century.
